units.translation: 476-83a. Of the Hamadryad nymph: Mnesimachus (fr. 3 M. IV 453) says that they are called Hamadryad nymphs because they are born together with the oaks; or because they are thought to perish together with the oaks, they are called Hamadryad nymphs. Charon of Lampsacus (fr. 12 M. I 35) relates that Rhoecus, seeing an oak that was on the point of falling to the ground, ordered his children to prop it up. The nymph who was about to perish along with the oak appeared to Rhoecus and said that she was grateful for her preservation, and allowed him to ask for whatever he wanted. When he asked to have intercourse with her, she promised to grant this; but she warned him to avoid intercourse with any other woman, and said that a bee would be a messenger between them. And once, while he was playing draughts, the bee flew up; and he made some rather harsh remark, which turned the nymph to anger, so that he was maimed. Pindar too, speaking about nymphs (fr. 165 Schr.), says: 'having obtained a token of a life equal to a tree's.' So the father of Paraebius, when cutting down an oak, was entreated by the nymph not to cut it; for since she had been born together with it, if it were cut down, she would be responsible for her own death. When he disobeyed, the divine power was angry with him and his descendants and became the cause of evils.

b. ἀϑέριξε: instead of 'he neglected.' Lg (P)
483-84. ἔγωγε μέν, εὖτ’ ἀφίκα〈νεν〉: To me, he says, when Paraebius came to consult the oracle and communicated his misfortune, I recognized that he was paying the penalty for his father's sin.
485a. λωφήια ῥέξαι: things by which the nymph's anger will abate and cease, that is, things to put an end to her anger.

b. λωφήια: propitiatory offerings, by which he will be relieved and cease from being afflicted. 'λωφῆσαι' is properly used of animals, meaning to put off the burden from the neck. And 'λωφήσων' (Aesch. Prom. 27) instead of 'will cease,' 'will rest the crest,' that is, the neck; or 'will rest.'
494. νέον ἤματος ἀνομένοιο: at dawn, when the day is increasing.
498-527a. ἦρι δ’ ἐτησίαι αὖραι: The Etesian winds begin to blow when the sun is in the last part of Cancer, until it passes Leo, as Aratus also says (Phaen. 151 ff.).
